turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry about the wait, we're running behind. The morning list got a bit messy.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, no stress, I was early. Parking by the robots was chaos, and with the builders I can't hear myself think out there, so coming inside was actually a relief.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shame. What has brought you in, then?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my face. I woke up and the one side is hanging, like the skin is just sliding down, and I don't look like myself in the mirror.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which side is hanging?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The left. I saw it when I brushed my teeth, about half past five, and I tried to whistle for the dog and nothing comes out, the air just leaks, I can't whistle at all.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Can you close the eye on that side?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I try and it stays open, it won't shut, and it waters the whole time. I feel like a wet rag, tired, and a bit shaky from the fright, if I'm honest.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, left face drooping since you woke, you can't whistle, and the left eye won't close. Any weakness in the arm or the leg?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I carried the washing in, both arms are normal, and the legs are fine. I got a fright because my uncle had a stroke, but everything else moves.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your speech, any slurring, or trouble getting the words out?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not at all. My sister says I sound exactly like myself, the words are all there, I'm not slurring. Sorry, I know I go on a bit.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before this morning, was there pain in the ear, or a rash?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, yesterday the left ear was sore, behind it, a deep ache. It's mostly settled, just a niggle now. No rash, I checked in the mirror more than once. I did wonder if I'd overdone it in the garden on Saturday.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you on any tablets at the moment?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I was on atorvastin, forty milligrams at night, for the cholesterol, but I stopped it in March. The pharmacy offered me ibuprofen yesterday for the ear and I never took it, not one tablet. They talked about a blood pressure tablet once and never actually gave it to me, so I don't take anything now.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cholesterol, statin stopped in March, nothing current, and you never started the ibuprofen or a blood pressure tablet. I'll examine the face.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Please. I've been trying to lift the eyebrow and the left one won't move at all, it's dead next to the right one. When I smile the mouth pulls right over to the good side, it's awful to look at.

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see it. The left forehead isn't moving, the left eye only closes about halfway, and the mouth is pulled to the right. Blood pressure is one thirty eight over eighty four, pulse seventy two. The arms are strong and equal, no weakness there.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a relief. My uncle was sixty two, my mother's brother, when he had the stroke, so it's been in my head all morning. I stay with my sister in Rondebosch and she spotted the face at breakfast before I said anything.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forehead involved, arms and speech spared. This looks like a Bell's palsy rather than a stroke. My first plan was a CT brain this morning, plus prednisone and aciclovir.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Aciclovir? I've never had a cold sore, and there's no blister, I really looked. I had a CT in February for a headache and they told me it was normal, my sister's got the letter. I'd rather not go in that machine again today if we can avoid it, I feel closed in.

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes it. No vesicles, forehead down, a recent normal scan, no limb signs. We'll leave the CT, and no aciclovir. I'll start prednisone, sixty milligrams by mouth once a day for five days, and then we taper.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty milligrams, once a day, for five days. Do I take it in the morning with food? I get heartburn if I take strong tablets on an empty stomach, it's been like that for years, really burns.

[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, morning, with food. For the eye, artificial tears about every hour while you're awake, and at night tape the left eye closed with micropore so it doesn't dry. Don't use a tight patch.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Every hour, tape at night, no tight patch. Will it come back, doctor? I'm meant to whistle the dog in and I can't, and I know that's a silly thing to fix on, sorry.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most people improve over a few weeks to months. I want you back here in three days to check the eye and the tablets. If the arm gets weak, or the speech changes, or the eye is very painful, come straight back the same day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days, and the same day if the arm or the speech or the eye goes bad. Can I start the prednisone today? The chemist by the clinic should have it, and the drops.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Start today, I'll write the script now. Forget the CT I mentioned, we're not booking it, and no antiviral. Just the steroid, the eye care, and I'll see you in three days.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Great, thank you. I'll fetch the drops and the tape, and I'll tell my sister so she stops panicking. See you in three days.

spec.situation: Person woke with one side of the face drooping, cannot close the eye, cannot whistle; no arm weakness, no speech problem, ear pain a day before; doctor examines and starts steroids, eye care explained.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

Medication history: a blood pressure tablet was discussed previously but was never actually started; patient currently takes no medicines.

Investigation/history relevant to management: patient had a CT in February for headache that was reportedly normal.
Eye-care instruction detail: tape the left eye closed with micropore at night and do not use a tight patch.
Follow-up detail: return in three days specifically to check the eye and the tablets.
Real disagreement/preference affecting plan: patient preferred to avoid another CT today because she feels closed in by the scanner; this contributed to the decision to leave the CT.
